pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 7-8. Understand that 100 is a bundle of ten tens (just as a ten is ten ones) — unitising climbs one level. Ten ten-rods fuse into one hundred-flat; 100 becomes a single countable unit.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 3): work in the number system to 1000; 'recognise the place value of each digit in a three-digit number (hundreds, tens, ones)' (this concept is its prerequisite unit).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT.1a '100 can be thought of as a bundle of ten tens — called a hundred'; foundation for 2.NBT.1.
• Operational details — Re-run the exact bundling story one order of magnitude up, using base-ten flats: count ten tens-rods, physically stack/overlay them onto one hundred-flat, and name the new unit. Stress the self-similar pattern (10 ones→1 ten; 10 tens→1 hundred) so children see place value as a repeating ×10 structure, not a list of separate facts.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7, emerging): builds 100 from ten tens-rods and says 'ten tens make one hundred'. Tier B (age 7-8, secure): explains 100 = 10 tens = 100 ones and treats a hundred-flat as one unit. Tier C (age 8, extending): articulates the repeating ×10 pattern and predicts the next unit (ten hundreds = one thousand).
bestPractices: Re-tell the SAME unitising story up a level with base-ten flats: ten tens-rods physically become one hundred-flat, mirroring ten ones → one ten.
Name the pattern explicitly: 'each new place is ten of the one before' — make the ×10 self-similarity the headline, not an incidental.
Hold three equivalent views of 100 together: 100 ones (a flat of little squares), 10 tens (ten rods), 1 hundred (one flat) — same quantity, different unit.
Anticipate the next rung (ten hundreds = a thousand) so the pattern is felt as open-ended.
Use the hundred-square (10×10 grid) as the bridge image between 'ten tens' and 'a hundred'.
keyRepresentations: Base-ten hundred-flat (10×10) vs ten tens-rods vs 100 unit-cubes — three views of 100
Hundred-square (10×10 grid) showing ten rows of ten
Gattegno / place-value chart adding the hundreds column
Bundled straws: ten bundles-of-ten wrapped into one bundle-of-hundred
commonMisconceptions: Thinking 100 is 'ten' with zeros, not literally ten tens or a hundred ones.
Failing to see the repeating ×10 structure — treating hundreds as an unrelated new idea.
Confusing a hundred-flat with a ten-rod (not tracking which unit is which).
Believing 100 ones and 10 tens are different amounts rather than the same quantity re-unitised.
Counting the little squares one-by-one instead of trusting the unit (no unitising).

learn.summary: For ages 7-8: understand that 100 is a bundle of ten tens, just as a ten is ten ones. The core proposed experience is watching ten ten-rods fuse into one hundred-flat, mirroring the earlier ten-ones-to-one-ten move, so children are intended to experience place value as a repeating ×10 structure rather than a list of separate facts. Hold three equivalent views of 100 together (100 single cubes, 10 rods, 1 flat), and foreshadow the next rung (ten hundreds make a thousand).

activities.title: Fuse ten tens into one hundred on an exchange bench
feedback: When the ten rods snap into one flat, confirm: 'Ten tens just became one hundred — the same move as ten ones becoming one ten, one level up.'
On the three-views toggle, point out the counter never moves: 'Still 100 — same amount, just re-unitised into a different unit.'
If a child treats the flat as unrelated to the rods, re-run the fuse and split slowly so they see the flat come apart into exactly ten rods.
Prompt the prediction: 'If ten tens make a hundred, what do you think ten hundreds make?'
activities.rationale: Performing the fuse/split action is intended to make unitising felt rather than merely stated, and re-running the same story one magnitude up is intended to surface the repeating ×10 structure. The merge animation together with a counter that stays steady at 100 is intended to make the equivalence concrete. Offered as a proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Place value is a self-similar ×10 structure; teaching should surface the repeating unitising pattern across ones/tens/hundreds.
100 can be thought of as a bundle of ten tens — called a 'hundred' (2.NBT.1a).
learnerActions: First re-bundle ten single ones into one ten-rod as a familiar recap, naming what happened: 'ten ones make one ten'.
Gather ten ten-rods into a staging tray; as the tenth rod lands, watch the ten rods merge into a single 10×10 hundred-flat.
Say aloud the pattern that connects the two moves: 'ten of the last unit always makes one of the next'.
Use a 'three views' toggle to flip the same hundred between 100 loose cubes, 10 rods, and 1 flat, while a counter stays steady at 100.
Look at a dimmed 'next level' shelf showing ten flats waiting to become a thousand-cube, and predict what comes next.
activities.intendedInsight: 100 is literally ten tens (and a hundred ones); each new place is ten of the one before, so place value is a self-similar ×10 pattern that keeps going.

activities.title: Bundle physical materials: ten tens into one hundred
feedback: If a child counts the rods and says 'ten', count the ones inside one rod (10), then skip-count the rods in tens to 100, naming 'ten tens, one hundred'.
If a child says 'twenty', distinguish 'ten AND ten' (which is 20) from 'ten LOTS of ten' (which is 100), then skip-count all ten rods to 100.
Reinforce by removing the materials and asking them to say '100 is ten tens' from memory.
activities.rationale: Base-ten equipment is genuinely 3D (cube→rod→flat→large cube), so handling real pieces or straw bundles can support unitising, and the hundred-square grid gives a stable bridge image. Offered as consolidation alongside the interactive fuse, not as evidence that any one medium is superior.
sourceClaims: 100 can be thought of as a bundle of ten tens — called a 'hundred' (2.NBT.1a).
learnerActions: Lay out ten ten-rods (or ten bundles-of-ten straws) and skip-count them: 10, 20, 30 … 100.
Physically stack or wrap all ten together and name the new unit: 'one hundred'.
State the three views in words: 100 ones, 10 tens, 1 hundred — the same quantity.
Overlay ten rods onto a 10×10 hundred-square grid to see ten rows of ten make the hundred.
activities.intendedInsight: A hundred built from real materials is the same quantity whether seen as 100 ones, 10 tens, or 1 hundred; the hundred-square bridges 'ten tens' and 'a hundred'.

activities.title: Match and complete the three views of 100
feedback: For 'ten tens = ___', accept 100 (or '1 hundred' / '100 ones', which name the same amount); for '100 = ___ tens', the answer is 10. If a child writes 100 for the number of tens, point back to the ten rods that made the flat.
If a child picks an option that is not equal to 100, lay the views side by side and count the tens together.
Ask the child to justify a correct match aloud so equivalence is reasoned, not guessed.
activities.rationale: Consolidation that checks the equivalence after the construction work. Recognition and fill-in confirm the stated equivalence but do not by themselves elicit the independent act of unitising, so they follow the hands-on activities.
sourceClaims: 100 can be thought of as a bundle of ten tens — called a 'hundred' (2.NBT.1a).
learnerActions: Match each representation to the others: 100 ↔ 10 tens ↔ 100 ones.
Choose which option is the same amount as 100 from a set of choices.
Explain in one sentence why each view is still 100.
activities.intendedInsight: The three views of 100 are equivalent, and the ×10 pattern can be stated, not just built.

constraints: The fuse/split construction should come before matching or fill-in tasks: recognition and completion check equivalence but do not elicit the independent act of unitising.

A static side-by-side reference (flat beside ten rods and 100 cubes with tap-to-reveal equivalences) is a useful anchor for the three views but does not let the child perform the fuse/split; use it to support, not replace, the hands-on move.

Paper, card, straw bundles and base-ten blocks have real (slight) thickness; a 2D screen flat is an idealised picture of the hundred-flat. Treat both as representations of the same quantity and name which unit each piece stands for.
Keep the 'next level' shelf (ten flats → thousand-cube) as an optional teaser to show the pattern is open-ended; do not require mastery of 1000 at this stage.

Diagnostic: show ten tens-sticks and ask what the bundled block is called, how many single ones it is, and how the child knows — the reason reveals ten-tens structure versus rote counting. Discriminating follow-up probes: 'How many single ones are there altogether in ten tens, and how could you be sure without counting them all?'; 'If I take one ten away, how many ones are left in the block now?'; 'Both 10 and 100 use the digits 1 and 0 — how are they different?'
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources (CCSS-M 2.NBT.1a and NCETM Primary Mastery) are marked unverified in the source row; the DfE Year 3 claim is marked verified. Comparative efficacy of any one medium is not established by these citations.
The DfE Year 3 claim is a curriculum/necessity statement about the objective rather than direct support for a specific teaching principle, so it is not used in activity sourceClaims.

The source row claimed 3D handling 'adds manipulation friction without insight' and that dialogue 'adds little'. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established facts; physical base-ten work is retained as a genuine activity and spoken reasoning (skip-counting aloud, justifying matches) is used within tasks.

Efficacy language in the summary and the interactive activity's rationale was softened to intended/proposed wording because the activities are unvalidated; an invented 'recolouring' visual not present in the original design notes was removed, keeping only the source's merge animation and steady counter.

Self-audit of arithmetic: ten tens = 100 ones (10 groups of 10); '10' tens (not 100) completes '100 = ___ tens', while '100' ones completes 'ten tens = ___'. 'Ten and ten' (20) differs from 'ten lots of ten' (100). These were checked; no erroneous value is left in any question or answer.

probeDeeper: How many single ones are there altogether in ten tens? How could you be sure without counting them all?
If I take one ten away, how many ones are left in the block now?
Both 10 and 100 use the digits 1 and 0 — how are they different?
assess.correctAnswer: One hundred. It is 100 ones altogether, because ten tens is 10 groups of 10, which makes 100.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts the sticks rather than their value: 'there are ten sticks so it's ten'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the ones inside one stick (10), then skip-count the sticks in tens: 10, 20 … 100. Name the new bundle 'one hundred = ten tens = a hundred ones'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child counts 1–10 across the sticks and answers 'ten'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds two tens instead of taking ten of them: 'ten and ten is twenty'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish 'ten AND ten' from 'ten LOTS of ten'. Skip-count all ten sticks in tens to 100.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reaches 100 only by counting every one, with no sense of the ten-tens structure
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the count — attach language to it: each time say '10, 20, 30 … that's ten tens, one hundred'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child laboriously counts all ones to 100 but cannot say '100 is ten tens' when asked again with sticks removed.

responseLevels.gap: Answers 'ten' (counts sticks) or 'twenty' (adds), showing no hundred-as-ten-tens unit.
responseLevels.full: Names the bundle 'one hundred', states it is ten tens and one hundred ones, and moves between the nested units (ones ⇄ tens ⇄ hundred).
responseLevels.partial: Reaches 100 but only by counting all the ones; cannot articulate that a hundred is ten tens.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show ten tens-sticks laid out. Ask: 'If I bundle all ten of these sticks together into one block, what is that block called, and how many single ones is it altogether? How do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has built the nested unit says 'a hundred' and knows it is 100 ones; a child counting only the visible sticks says 'ten' (counts the sticks, not their value), and an additive thinker says 'twenty' (10 + 10). The reason tier reveals whether they reach 100 by the ten-tens structure or by rote.
